t: Gnostic groups held that a hidden supreme being stood above a flawed creator, the demiurge, and that salvation came through direct knowledge (gnosis) of one's own divine origin.
For centuries it was known mainly through the hostile writings of Church Fathers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus, until the Nag Hammadi library was found in Egypt in 1945.
Scholars now debate whether "Gnosticism" is a form of early Christianity, a category created by its opponents or a tradition in its own right, and many question its use as a single label.
dyk: The Nag Hammadi library, twelve leather-bound papyrus codices sealed in a jar, was found in 1945 by a local farmer, Muhammed al-Samman, and may have belonged to a nearby Pachomian monastery.
ev: Marcion of Sinope preaches in Rome, is expelled and starts a congregation that spreads through the Mediterranean
Irenaeus writes Against Heresies (c. 180–185), which names Simon Magus as the inceptor of Gnosticism
Mani travels to the Indo-Greek Kingdom of the Sakas in what is now Afghanistan (240–241), before joining the court of Shapur I
Bishop Athanasius condemns the use of non-canonical books in his Festal Letter, after which the Nag Hammadi codices may have been buried
Manichaeism becomes the state religion of the Uyghur Khaganate
The Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) begins; it and conversion to Islam greatly reduced the remaining Gnostics of the Middle Ages
Jules Doinel re-establishes a Gnostic church in France
The Nag Hammadi library is found near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt

f.origin: the Mediterranean world, with Alexandria central to its birth; the origins cannot be traced exactly and are disputed, and the systems were fully developed by the mid-2nd century
f.founder: none: a collection of groups and teachers, among them Valentinus (c. 100 – c. 180), Basilides of Alexandria and Marcion, rather than one founder
f.scriptures: the Nag Hammadi library of 1945, with fifty-two mostly Gnostic treatises in Coptic, including the Gospel of Thomas and the Apocryphon of John; the Mandaean Ginza Rabba; and the reports of Church Fathers such as Irenaeus
f.followers: Mandaeans, thought to number 60,000 to 70,000 worldwide, in Iraq, Iran and diaspora communities, and small modern Gnostic churches
